newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Refugees flee after eastern Zaire fighting.
newsitem.headline: Refugees flee after eastern Zaire fighting.

text.p: About 46,000 refugees deserted two camps near Zaire's border with Burundi after a flare-up of fighting between Zairean soldiers and ethnic Tutsi rebels, relief workers said.
A special envoy from U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali was due to visit eastern Zaire on Sunday to monitor the situation.

Relief workers in the South Kivu regional capital of Bukavu said the envoy, Ibrahima Fall, would try to cool passions in the volatile border zone where at least 28 civilians were killed and 17 wounded in clashes on Friday.

Elsewhere, military sources said Zairean soldiers were being resupplied with heavy weapons to respond to attacks by ethnic Tutsi Banyamulenge, whom Zaire says were sent by Rwanda via Burundi to destablise the area.
Relief workers in Rwanda's capital Kigali said refugees had fled from two camps near the border town of Uvira.
"The populations of both Kagunga and Runingo, some 46,000 refugees, have all moved," said Paul Stromberg, spokesman for the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees in Rwanda.
"Fighting has broken out this morning between the Banyamulenge and Zairean armed forces near Luvengi refugee camp."

Hundreds of thousands of Hutu refugees who fled to Zaire from Rwanda, fearing reprisals after the 1994 massacres of minority Tutsis by Hutu hardliners there. Other Hutu refugees fled similar ethnic conflict in Burundi.
It was unclear whether the Tutsi Banyamulenge had attacked Hutu camps. A senior Zairean military commander spoke only of fighting near the camp.
About 220,000 Rwandan and Burundian refugees languish in 12 camps north of Uvira, a town near Burundi in the delta to the northwest of Lake Tanganyika.

The Banyamulenge, who arrived in Zaire from Rwanda in the late 18th century, say they are fighting for their right to Zairean citizenship. They say indigenous Zaireans discriminate against them on the basis of language and ethnicity.

The Zairean commander said Banyamulenge from Rwanda's army crossed the border from Burundi on Friday. "When they arrived they opened fire with light arms on the local population living in villages around Kiliba," he said.
Stromberg said some refugees from the two camps had gone "to Uvira, some into the hills above Uvira, some into banana plantations and the remainder have dispersed."
Aid workers in Uvira were confined to their houses by street protests by Zaireans criticising the United Nations and denouncing the Banyamulenge.
Switzerland said Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko could stay after a temporary visa expired on October 27 if he needed more treatement for cancer.
Diplomats fear that Mobutu's prolonged absence will fuel chaos in Zaire and lead to a wider conflict in Central Africa.
